hops.afterHeading: Build one circuit, then test the tool
hops.title: Why ordinary mice are less sensitive to diphtheria toxin
hops.text: Human cells are far more sensitive to diphtheria toxin than mouse cells are. The toxin has to dock onto a membrane-anchored growth factor, HB-EGF, before it can shut down protein synthesis, and amino acid substitutions in the mouse version spoil the fit. In 2001 Saito and colleagues put the human receptor into mouse liver cells; injected toxin damaged those cells, with no obvious abnormalities in other tissues in that experiment. Later work showed the toxin also reaches the central nervous system. Duan and colleagues expressed the receptor in genetically marked neurons; toxin depleted 82 percent of labelled lumbar dorsal-cord neurons and depleted labelled neurons in the hindbrain spinal trigeminal nucleus.

hops.title: Why nearby touch dulls pain more than distant touch
hops.text: Notice where your hand goes the instant you bang a shin on a coffee table: straight to the skin beside the bump, not to the other leg. Does it matter where the touch lands? Mancini and colleagues put light touches on either side of a painful laser pulse on volunteers' forearms, 1, 5 or 9 centimetres away. At 1 and 5 centimetres people had more trouble telling two pulse strengths apart and leaned toward the lower rating; at 9 centimetres that lean was not detected. In a separate hand experiment, nearby touch weakened a blink reflex generated in the brainstem, so some of the gating sits below the cortex.

sources.citation: Mancini F, Nash T, Iannetti GD, Haggard P. Pain. 2014;155(3):635-642. PMCID: PMC3988987.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student sitting on a sofa gently rubbing one shin next to a wooden coffee table.
image.caption: Nearby touch biased pain ratings lower, with no clear shift at 9 centimetres; separately, nearby touch weakened a brainstem reflex.

hops.title: The substance-P blocker that prevents chemotherapy vomiting
hops.text: In the 1990s drug companies tested blockers of NK1r, the substance-P receptor carried by most mouse lumbar lamina I neurons traced from the lateral parabrachial area. In animals the blockers damped sensitized pain responses; in human pain trials the class disappointed. Substance P also acts in brainstem circuits involved in vomiting, and L-754,030 cut vomiting in ferrets. In a 1999 cisplatin trial where everyone received standard day-one antinausea drugs, 82 percent given L-754,030 before chemotherapy and through day five had neither vomiting nor retching on days two to five, versus 33 percent given placebo from day one through day five. It reached the clinic in 2003 as aprepitant.

audio.title: Three Stories Behind the Tools in This Lesson
audio.transcript: Some of the best stories in spinal pain research hide inside the tools rather than the circuits. Here are three. Start with the chloride problem. To tell which way a chloride current will move a lamina one neuron's voltage, you measure where that current reverses and compare that reversal potential with the neuron's starting membrane potential. The trouble is that in a conventional whole-cell recording, the cell's chloride exchanges with the pipette solution, so the gradient you wanted to measure drifts toward the one you poured into the glass. The fix came out of a jar of dirt. At the Rockefeller Institute in the late nineteen thirties, the soil microbiologist Rene Dubos spent two years feeding soil samples a diet of staphylococci, pneumococci and streptococci, betting that ordinary soil already held microbes built to destroy them. Out came a spore-forming bacterium, Bacillus brevis, and with the biochemist Rollin Hotchkiss he pulled gramicidin out of it, the first antibiotic agent ever tested in the clinic. It was too toxic to put into a vein, so it went onto surface wounds instead, and Howard Florey credited Dubos's work with reviving his own stalled penicillin research. Then in nineteen ninety-five, electrophysiologists recording from cultured rat dorsal-horn neurons used gramicidin to open pores that pass sodium and potassium while leaving chloride where it was. A soil antibiotic from the nineteen thirties is what lets spinal chloride speak for itself. Second story: the tidy rule that inhibitory transmitters always hyperpolarize is not a rule. In some immature neurons chloride builds up inside, because the transporter N K C C one helps bring chloride in while the exporter K C C two becomes prominent only as those neurons mature. That buildup can make the chloride equilibrium potential more positive, so when chloride channels open while the starting membrane potential is more negative than that equilibrium potential, chloride leaves and depolarizes the cell. There is a clinical pattern that sent researchers looking at this: in some newborns, visible seizure movements stop after treatment while electrical seizure activity carries on underneath. In two thousand five, researchers found that bumetanide, a chloride-importer blocker, shifted the reversal potential of GABA-evoked currents more negative in neonatal rat hippocampal slices and, in a separate in vivo experiment in that paper, reduced electrical seizure activity in neonatal rats with induced seizures. Note what the gradient does and does not settle: it helps set which way the voltage moves, and even a depolarizing response can still dampen other inputs. Third, the designer drug that was not silent. When researchers evolved muscarinic receptors for chemogenetics in yeast in two thousand seven, they chose clozapine-N-oxide, or C N O, in part because it looked pharmacologically inert, and labs often used it as though it were. By two thousand sixteen, researchers had reported behavioural effects in rats given C N O. In two thousand seventeen, researchers saw little brain uptake of labelled C N O in rats and weaker receptor binding than clozapine, while later mouse work found that free C N O can reach cerebrospinal fluid levels high enough to activate an inhibitory engineered receptor. Still, some C N O converts into clozapine, an antipsychotic that enters the brain readily and can act on both engineered and native receptors. In two thousand twenty-three, researchers found that C N O altered sleep in male mice without engineered receptors: over six hours, the middle and higher doses reduced R E M as a share of total sleep, with no statistically significant overall change in R E M as a share of recording time. The lesson is older than chemogenetics: interrogate the tool as hard as you interrogate the circuit.
